All rights reserved. Page 2 Stonewater Group Internal Overview — Confidential 1. The Opportunity Most commercial real estate sponsors operate in a similar fashion. Deal flow initiates the decision-making process: a site surfaces, underwriting begins, and capital follows. Capital allocation is driven more by what becomes available than by a defined view of where and how to invest. The result is a process that never compounds. Assumptions vary by deal and by analyst. Decisions are made without a common framework. Over time, the portfolio reflects opportunity and timing more than deliberate strategy — and the organization doesn't get systematically better at making decisions. The most intentional operators take a different approach. They establish a thesis before evaluating deals — a deliberate view on where to deploy capital, why, and under what conditions. Opportunities are measured against that thesis rather than evaluated in isolation. Each deal sharpens the process rather than restarting it. Stonewater Group provides the frameworks, analysis, and tools that allow sponsors to make that shift — from deal-driven to thesis-driven. Our services standardize how markets are selected, how opportunities are evaluated, and how capital is allocated, replacing ad hoc decision-making with a repeatable process that improves over time. For sponsors, the practical benefits of operating this way are direct: stronger capital relationships built on a credible and legible investment process, better risk-adjusted decisions through consistent underwriting and market selection, and a platform that scales without decision quality degrading. Thesis-driven sponsors don't just win more deals — they win better ones, and they build the kind of track record that attracts institutional capital over time. That shift — from deal-driven to thesis-driven — is what Stonewater Group is built to support. © Stonewater Group. All rights reserved. Page 3 Stonewater Group Internal Overview — Confidential 2. About Us Stonewater Group is a real estate advisory firm. We work with multifamily and mixed-use development sponsors across the United States, providing the decision-making infrastructure that allows them to evaluate markets, underwrite opportunities, and manage capital with institutional-grade discipline. Our work is delivered through consulting and advisory engagements. We do not take equity positions, manage assets directly, or act as a principal in transactions. Our role is to provide the frameworks, analysis, and structured deliverables that clients need to make better decisions — and to build the internal processes that make those decisions repeatable. We focus exclusively on ground-up multifamily development. This focus is intentional. It allows us to go deep on the specific analytical and strategic challenges that development sponsors face, and to build a knowledge base that compounds across clients and markets over time. At any given time, Stonewater concentrates its market coverage on a defined set of geographies. This allows our research, relationships, and market intelligence to compound in specific places rather than being spread thin across too many markets simultaneously. Coverage will expand as the firm grows. 3. How We Work Stonewater's services are organized in five-phases — forming a connected framework that mirrors how thesis-driven sponsors evaluate, approve, and manage development opportunities from market selection through exit. Clients can engage Stonewater in two ways: Individual Deliverables © Stonewater Group. All rights reserved. Page 4 Stonewater Group Internal Overview — Confidential Clients can engage Stonewater for a specific analysis or advisory need — underwriting a deal, evaluating a market, or preparing investment committee materials. Each deliverable is scoped, priced, and delivered independently. Investment Operating System Clients can engage Stonewater across multiple phases, allowing each deliverable to build on the prior one. This approach mirrors how institutional firms allocate capital, approve deals, and manage assets over time. It produces the greatest value because decisions made within a connected framework are more consistent and comparable across deals. Most client relationships begin with a single, discrete deliverable — a market study, a deal screen, or an underwriting model — scoped to address a specific and immediate need. Over time, as additional phases are completed, these individual engagements compound into a fully integrated Investment Operating System. Engagement Process Every engagement follows a consistent process regardless of scope: Discovery — Stonewater initiates each engagement with a structured discovery conversation to understand the client's current pipeline, operational priorities, and where their existing process has gaps. This conversation defines the scope, timeline, and deliverable format before any work begins. Delivery — All deliverables are completed within a defined timeline and delivered in a structured, professional format. Upon delivery, Stonewater conducts a dedicated review session with the client to walk through findings, address questions, and document decisions made as a result of the analysis. Next Steps — The review session is used to identify what the logical next engagement is based on where the client is in their pipeline and what the completed deliverable surfaced. Expansion into additional phases happens organically as the client's needs evolve. 4. Who We Serve © Stonewater Group. All rights reserved. Lenders The lender client base includes financial institutions and private credit providers extending construction financing to multifamily development sponsors — regional and community banks, private debt funds, bridge lenders, and specialty lenders. 5. Investment Operating System The Investment Operating System (IOS) is Stonewater's core framework. It is organized into five phases, each building on the prior one. Together, they constitute a repeatable decision system that spans the full development lifecycle. Phase I — Thesis Formation Capital allocation begins before a single deal is evaluated. Phase I establishes a market strategy framework that defines where to deploy capital and why — prioritizing metros and submarkets using standardized scoring methodologies built around demographic trends, supply dynamics, rent growth, affordability, and cycle positioning. Outcome: Sponsors enter markets with a documented, defensible rationale — reducing exposure to poorly timed or structurally weak market entries. © Stonewater Group. All rights reserved. Page 6 Stonewater Group Internal Overview — Confidential Phase II — Deal Sourcing Before advancing any deal to full underwriting, each opportunity is tested against a standardized screening framework — minimum return thresholds, basis assumptions, risk flags, and feasibility benchmarks. Only deals that clear this bar move forward. Outcome: Internal resources are concentrated on opportunities with genuine return potential, and weak deals are identified early before significant time or capital is committed. Phase III — Underwriting & Feasibility Phase III is the analytical core of the IOS. Site-specific market analysis and institutional- grade financial modeling are conducted under standardized assumptions for rents, costs, absorption, and exit conditions. Every deal concludes with a structured risk assessment and a clear recommendation — approve, approve with conditions, or decline. Outcome: Decision-makers have a complete, consistent picture of each deal's risk and return profile — giving them the confidence to commit capital or the clarity to walk away. Phase IV — Capital Raising & Packaging With underwriting complete and a deal approved, Phase IV translates the investment thesis into materials that can withstand external scrutiny. Deliverables are structured to support conversations with construction lenders, equity partners, and institutional capital providers. Outcome: Sponsors enter capital conversations with professionally packaged, analytically supported materials — improving credibility with lenders and equity partners and reducing friction in the financing process. Phase V — Asset Management As real performance data replaces projections, Stonewater provides ongoing oversight of asset performance, capital structure, and liquidity positioning — continuously benchmarking results against original underwriting assumptions. Lessons learned feed back into future market selection and underwriting processes. Outcome: Underperformance is identified early, capital obligations are actively monitored, and the platform's decision-making improves with each completed deal. © Stonewater Group. All rights reserved. Page 7 Stonewater Group Internal Overview — Confidential Value of Integrated, Thesis-Driven System Proprietary Intelligence — Over time, the IOS builds a documented body of market intelligence, underwriting history, and performance data specific to the sponsor’s platform — institutional knowledge that is difficult to replicate and becomes a durable competitive advantage. Credibility — When lenders or equity partners question an assumption, the answer is a formal analysis that predates the deal — not a defense constructed to support it. Accelerated Deal Evaluation — With market selection criteria, screening thresholds, and underwriting assumptions established in advance, each new opportunity is evaluated against a standing framework rather than assembled from scratch. Standardized Analysis — Consistent assumptions across deals allow sponsors to compare return profiles, risk assessments, and market conclusions on the same terms across every opportunity in the pipeline. Compounding Feedback Loop — Actual performance benchmarked against original projections reveals where assumptions are systematically off, and those corrections are applied to future underwriting before capital is committed. 6. Competitive Landscape Sponsors seeking analytical and advisory support for ground-up multifamily development typically encounter four categories of providers. Large national advisory firms — firms such as CBRE, Newmark, and Colliers offer broad capability across capital markets, brokerage, valuation, and advisory. Their advisory practices are primarily oriented around transactions — acquisition, disposition, and debt placement — rather than the development decision-making process. Engagements are typically structured for institutional clients with large, complex mandates. Specialized research and feasibility firms — firms such as RCLCO, John Burns Research and Consulting, and MRC deliver market research, feasibility studies, and demand analysis. Their work is typically scoped to a single question — market feasibility for a specific site, demand analysis for a specific product type — rather than structured as an integrated framework across the full development lifecycle. Independent consultants and freelancers — a fragmented category of practitioners offering underwriting, market analysis, and advisory support on a project-by-project basis. Engagements are flexible and accessible but are not typically supported by proprietary frameworks, standardized methodologies, or continuity across a client's deal pipeline. Internal development staff — sponsors who build analytical capacity in-house through dedicated analysts or development associates. This model provides continuity but requires fixed overhead, and specialized functions rarely justify dedicated headcount at most platform sizes. Stonewater operates in a distinct position within this landscape — focused exclusively on ground-up multifamily development, structured around the full investment lifecycle rather than individual transactions, and built to produce consistent, comparable outputs across a client's deal pipeline over time. 9. Ben may attend review sessions at principal discretion. 10. Go-to-Market Strategy Stonewater's near-term client acquisition strategy is focused exclusively on multifamily developers. Investor and lender client development will be pursued once a developer client base is established. Stonewater pursues new business through four channels operating in parallel. Direct Outreach Stonewater conducts targeted outreach to decision-makers at multifamily development firms via LinkedIn and email. Outreach is focused on founders, principals, and senior development executives at firms actively pursuing ground-up development. The goal of each outreach sequence is to initiate a discovery conversation rather than pitch a specific deliverable. Content Stonewater publishes a quarterly market report on its website. Each report is gated — available for download in exchange for contact information — and is supported by a distribution campaign across LinkedIn and X. Content is designed to demonstrate analytical capability, build brand credibility, and drive inbound traffic from sponsors actively researching markets Stonewater covers. The contact information collected through report downloads feeds directly into the outreach pipeline. © Stonewater Group. All rights reserved. Page 15 Stonewater Group Internal Overview — Confidential Referrals Stonewater maintains active relationships with existing personal connections and past clients, with a deliberate focus on generating introductions to development firms that fit the target client profile. Every completed engagement is treated as a referral opportunity — the review session at delivery is used to identify whether the client has peers or partners who could benefit from Stonewater's services. Upwork Upwork serves as an early-stage lead generation and credibility-building channel. The objective is not to build a large Upwork client base but to accumulate verified reviews and completed engagements that validate Stonewater's capabilities to prospective clients outside the platform. Strong Upwork clients are transitioned to direct engagements over time. Client Development The objective of each initial engagement is to demonstrate enough value to generate a second. Stonewater's engagement model — discrete, fixed-fee deliverables with a structured delivery and review process — is designed to reduce the friction of a first engagement and create a natural on-ramp to broader IOS relationships over time. A client who engages Stonewater for a single market study and receives a thorough, well-documented analysis is the most effective sales tool the firm has. 11. Goals & Strategic Direction Long-Term Vision Stonewater's advisory practice is designed to build toward something larger than a consulting business. Every client engagement, completed deliverable, and capital conversation is an opportunity to establish credibility and deepen relationships with the developers, investors, and lenders who will become Stonewater's future co-GP partners, LP relationships, and lending partners. The advisory business is the vehicle through which that network is built and that track record is established. The long-term objective is to leverage Stonewater's advisory relationships and market expertise into active participation in multifamily development — as a co-GP, capital partner, or principal investor alongside the clients and partners the firm serves. While the broader Franklin / Cool Springs market has demonstrated the ability to absorb new supply, recent lease-up performance and rent trends indicate increasing sensitivity to unit size, pricing, and product differentiation—particularly among large, undifferentiated Class A apartment communities. Rather than competing directly with existing and planned podium and garden apartment developments, the recommended program intentionally re- segments renter demand across three complementary formats: big-house quadplexes, farm-style clustered multifamily, and town-center stacked flats over retail. This approach allows the project to appeal to a wider range of renter profiles—downsizers, young families, and lifestyle-oriented professionals—while reducing reliance on any single renter cohort or rent band. Importantly, the program aligns with observed market behavior showing strong and durable demand for home-oriented rental product that offers greater privacy, space, and character than traditional apartments, while remaining more attainable than for-sale housing. By phasing delivery and sequencing lower-risk, missing-middle product ahead of higher-density mixed-use components, the development strategy mitigates near-term lease- up risk while preserving long-term value and rent durability consistent with a core+ hold profile. The subject site is best positioned as a farm-forward, village-scale rental community within a larger ±192-acre mixed-use agrihood, rather than as a conventional suburban multifamily or mixed-use development. The core value proposition is not density or amenity concentration, but authentic place-making anchored by real agricultural production, walkability, and a human-scaled town center. This positioning directly responds to growing renter demand for purpose-driven communities that offer daily-life engagement, authenticity, and connection to land—attributes largely absent from the existing competitive inventory in the Franklin / Cool Springs market. Importantly, the project’s integration with a working farm, trail network, village retail, and future hospitality offering elevates the rental component from a standalone housing product to a supporting use within a broader living ecosystem. This supports long- term value creation consistent with a core+ hold strategy, while phasing allows the project to establish identity and demand before delivering higher- density, town-center-adjacent product. The financing is intended to refinance existing debt, enhance capital structure efficiency, and facilitate orderly asset‑level monetization. Approximately $18.7 million will be funded at closing to refinance existing loans, of which ~$6.0 million to be structured as a revolving credit facility ("Revolver") towards governed townhome construction draws. Approximately $1.2 Million will fund an interest reserve account at close to be applied towards paymentsfor the 1st Seven (7) months. Interest will accue on the total loan balance inclusive of the interest reserve.Sponsor equity at close represents costs outside of the loan proceeds (Origination fee to the lender & estimated legal/closing costs); substantial prior land and infrastructure equity is embedded in the collateral. Primary repayment is expected from 51 substantially completed Phase III lots under executed purchase agreements with rolling takedowns, underwritten conservatively to a 12‑month sell‑off generating approximately $22.0 million of net proceeds, sufficient to fully repay the lot tranche, which will include minimum interest protection. Restaurant Row, consisting of two retail buildings with leasing underway and an ~$11.0 million cost basis, provides secondary and tertiary repayment support through refinance or sale but is not required for base‑case repayment. The townhome component supports Phase I development of 21 permit‑ready units, structured as a controlled revolver with an 85% sales‑based release, with approximately 12 units underwritten for sale within the initial term; land is underwritten at as‑is value only. Repayment shall be structured through a lender‑controlled, multi‑source waterfall comprised of lot sales, governed townhome unit sales, and retail refinance or disposition. RECOMMENDATION We recommend structuring the financing as a Single, Cross‑Collateralized Senior Credit Facility with Internally Segmented Tranches, rather than a traditional unitranche with a blended coupon. This approach provides unified lender control while allowing each tranche to be priced, amortized, and managed according to its specific asset risk and repayment profile. The underlying collateral pools exhibit materially different characteristics and exit paths. Phase III lots are presold and expected to amortize through rolling takedowns; Restaurant Row retail is subject to lease‑up and refinance risk; and the townhome land and construction exposure carries longer‑duration execution and absorption risk. Economically segmenting the facility preserves proper risk‑based pricing, repayment mechanics, covenant calibration, and workout flexibility without sacrificing administrative efficiency. Given the fast‑pay potential of the lot collateral, the Phase III tranche should include a Minimum Interest or Yield‑Protection Mechanism to ensure the lender is adequately compensated for early repayment risk and for the control value provided to the broader facility. A blended unitranche structure would obscure asset‑level risk differences, create implicit subsidies across collateral types, and reduce transparency in ongoing asset management. A multi‑tranche structure under one facility more accurately reflects the economic reality of the project while preserving cross‑collateralization, unified enforcement rights, and a streamlined borrower interface. Investment Thesis Marketplace at Altamonte represents an opportunity to develop 384 Class A multifamily units on a uniquely entitled 24-acre infill site in Altamonte Springs, a high-growth Seminole County submarket with demonstrably strong renter demand and a tapering new supply pipeline. At a stabilized yield on cost of 5.87% — a positive spread to the 5.25% going-in cap rate — Phase 1 generates immediate value creation from day one without relying on aggressive exit assumptions to justify the equity deployment. The low-rise program at $250/SF positions the project competitively on a cost basis relative to recently delivered mid-rise comps in the submarket, and the 80-unit/acre entitlement across the remaining site provides a durable source of long-term land value independent of Phase 1 performance. The 12% LIRR hurdle is achievable under a base-case scenario of 2.5% annual rent growth and modest cap rate compression through a 5-year hold, with the promote structure appropriately aligned to LP return expectations for a suburban Florida new construction deal. The thesis rests on two assumptions: GC validation of the $250/SF hard cost basis, and land acquisition at or near the market-supported range — either deviating materially would compress the YOC below the level needed to clear the equity hurdle on a standalone basis.
